The second case, also tried just previous to the holiday recess, concerned four calls, three of which were charged to the Chi Phi fraternity house, and one to the Kappa Sigma fraternity house. This student, also, was found guilty by his own admission.

Placed on Parole
He was placed on good conduct parole for the remainder of the year and fined $50, $25 of which was suspended. A letter was also sent to his parents.

The student stated that his fraternity had been charged with approximately $250 worth of illegal long distance calls last year, and that he had heard of others doing it and getting away with it. He further declared that he did not feel that these facts justified his action and that he did think he would eventually be caught.

In addition to penalties levied by the court, both men were required to pay for the cost of the calls made and for the expense of tracing them to determine the identity of the caller.

More Cases Pending
Rog Thaler, chief justice of the court, told the Transcript that more cases are pending and will be handled before the end of the semester.

In each case the Northern Ohio Telephone Co. sent a report of the violations, along with names of students involved, to Dean of Student Personnel Services Allan C. Ingraham, who turned the charges over to Assistant Dean of Men Paul Engsberg. The cases were then given to Men's Court for its decision.

Thaler also pointed out that, as stated in the Ohio Wesleyan Student Handbook of rules and regulations, placing a phone call under a false or assumed name constitutes a federal offense and is punishable, if tried in federal court, by a $200 fine or six months imprisonment or both.

Tolls Were Charged To Other Groups

Men's Court found two members of the sophomore class guilty of "conduct unbecoming an Ohio Wesleyan student" after they were convicted of placing and falsely charging long distance phone calls recently.

Court recorder Robbin Farrar disclosed details of the case to the Transcript, withholding names in accordance with Men's Court policy.

The calls were placed under assumed names and were charged to Ohio Wesleyan fraternities of which the guilty parties were not members.

Phi Delts Victimized

The first case, tried the week preceding Christmas vacation, involved one call charged to the Phi Delta Theta fraternity house. The student was found guilty by his own admission and placed on good conduct parole until the end of the 1959-60 academic year. He was also fined $25.

The man involved in this case stated to the court that the act was not premeditated, and that he wanted to call his parents. articles.headline: Washington Conference Invites OWU
articles.body:
White House Hosts; SC Picks OWU Rep

Ohio Wesleyan University has been invited to send a student delegate to a White House Conference on Children and Youth, Student Body President Bryce Collier announced last week. Donald Irish, associate professor of sociology at OWU, has already been chosen to represent the Delaware area.

This is the sixth conference of its type, and will be held from Mar. 27 to Apr. 2 at the University of Maryland.

Council To Choose

Collier explained that the delegate would be selected by Student Council at the next meeting (yesterday) from a list of names of people who were recommended by Student Council members or who indicated their interest in the conference.

As the entire cost of the trip will probably total about $250, Student Government will provide $200 for the delegate's expenses. Student Council hopes that the University will provide the remainder of the necessary funds, Collier said.

Of the 165 people who will represent Ohio at the conference, only 16 are college students, Collier said. The adult representatives were chose on the basis of population distribution.

Began In 1909

The White House Conferences were begun in 1909 by by Theodore Roosevelt. Since then, the President who has been in office at the turn of each decade has called a conference.

The subjects discussed will range from the effects of scientific developments and population pressures on children to the extent of the impact of today's economics and culture on child welfare, Collier said.

articles.headline: 25 Students Become Undergrad Fellows

The list of 25 students is 9 members smaller than that of the first semester because of limited funds, according to Ronald R. Greene, professor of psychology, and chairman of the Committee on Honors.

articles.headline: Special Grant Goes To Kelly
articles.body:
J. B. Kelly, associate professor of history and political science, received a special grant-in-aid for research from the Social Science Research Council in New York last week.

Prof. Kelly will travel to London next August to collect material for a diplomatic history of Iran in the 1800-1914 period. He has already gathered nearly half of his needed material, and the one-year grant will allow him to finish his research. At that time he will return to the U.S. to write his book at the expiration of the grant.

The open-end fellowship will pay for a year's salary, traveling expenses and research costs, including secretarial help, Prof. Kelly stated. The faculty research program is jointly operated by the SSRC and the American Council of Learned Societies.

Before using the scholarship, Prof. Kelly will teach a graduate course in Modern Middle East history at a joint summer school held every year by the five universities east of the Mississippi having departments in Middle Eastern affairs.

vard, Columbia, Michigan and Johns Hopkins Universities.

Prof. Kelly came from Oxford, England, in 1958, where he had been a lecturer since 1955. He received his Ph.D. at London University in 1955 and was a Research Fellow in history at the Institute of Historical Research there concurrently. He has traveled through most of the Middle East and lived several years there.

Prof. Kelly has published several articles on Arabia and the Persian Gulf. "Sultanate and Imamate in Oman" will be published by the Royal Institute of International Affairs this month, he said.

At the moment, Prof. Kelly of this year, according to is working on history of British policy in the Persian Gulf area in the 19th century. The book will be completed by spring and published the end Prof. Kelly.

Speaking of his two years here, Prof. Kelly commented, "I've quite enjoyed it."

articles.headline: COURSE DROPPED
articles.body:
The Administration has decided to discontinue OWU's Middle Eastern studies program next year because of budgetary considerations, J. B. Kelly, associate professor of history and political science, announced Sunday.

Prof. Kelly's appointment to initiate the program two years ago will be terminated in June.

articles.headline: SG To Print Candidates' Qualifications
articles.body:
Holy Day Forces Schedule Change

Student Government will publish a brochure listing the qualifications of candidates for Student Government offices this spring in an effort to equalize expenditures of sponsoring organizations, Dave Fisher, Elections Committee chairman, has announced.

Each candidate will be restricted to publishing only one campaign bulletin. Qualifications are not to be included in this bulletin, stressed Fisher, since they will be listed in the brochure.

The new restrictions on campaign literature are part of a series of changes which the Elections Committee hopes will increase student interest in SG elections and equalize candidates' chances, Fisher stated. No restrictions will be made on campaign expenditures, as previous restrictions have been ineffective, he said.

Candidates Must Register

Students wishing to run for office this year may do so by registering with Student Council and paying a small fee, said Fisher. The final registration date has not yet been decided, he said.

Last year, nominations were made during a special nominating Chapel. This spring, however, the date for the nominating Chapel fell on Ash Wednesday, Mar. 2, resulting in the cancellation of nominations. (see Transcript, Oct. 14.)

Rally Being Considered

The possibility of a nominating rally in the gym or a convention-type meeting in Gray Chapel that Wednesday evening is being considered, said Fisher. An effort will also be made to provide more MUB round-table discussions and opportunities for candidates to speak at dinner in fraternity houses and dormitories.

Election day will be Mar. 7, with the polls open all day. On Mar. 4 a "Meet-the-Candidates Chapel" is scheduled at which all the candidates will give their final speeches, concluded Fisher.

articles.headline: Easton Is Nominated For Nat'l AAUP Post
articles.body:
Loyd D. Easton, professor of philosophy, has been nominated for a national office in the American Association of University Professors, it was learned last week.

The national AAUP Nominating Committee chose Prof. Easton and Notre Dame Economics Professor Paul A. Montavon as candidates for the District 6 post on its 10-man National Council.

District 6 includes all colleges with AAUP chapters in Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Illinois and Kentucky. AAUP's National Council has one representative each from 10 districts, which include all 50 states, the District of Columbia, 8 Canadian provinces, the Panama Canal Zone and Puerto Rico.

Elections are held by mail ballot between now and Mar. 1; results will be announced at the national convention later in the spring.

Prof. Easton, who has been chairman of the Philosophy Department since 1952, is a former president of OWU's chapter of AAUP, and he has held other local and regional posts with the organization.

articles.headline: 5 College Groups To Hold Midwinter Meeting Here
articles.body:
A midwinter week end sponsored by the Five College Conference will be held at OWU Feb. 19-21, Conference Committee Chairman Jane Polley has announced. Sixty-100 delegates from Antioch, Denison, Oberlin and Wooster are expected to arrive Friday evening and will be housed in the dormitories and fraternity houses.

Conferences will be held on Saturday afternoon, Miss Polley said. These conferences will be divided into several discussion groups concerning both campus affairs and subjects of broader scope which interest college students, she added.

Miss Polley stated that she will interview any students interested in positions as group discussion chairmen during the first week of next semester. Students may sign up for interviews Feb. 1-3 in the Student Government Office in the MUB.

Miss Polley also announced tentative plans for the rest of the conference week end. On Friday evening, one of the participating schools will present entertainment open to all OWU students. Delegates may attend classes Saturday morning. On Saturday night a conference banquet will be held in the MUB. A convocation will be held Sunday morning for the delegates.

articles.headline: Senior Tests Under Way
articles.body:
94 Take First OWU Comprehensives

The University-wide dry run comprehensive examination program for seniors moved ahead rapidly last Saturday with 94 seniors in seven different departments taking nationally standardized tests provided by the Educational Testing Service, Princeton, N. J.

Fifty economics majors, nine French majors, nine physics majors, nine sociology majors, six philosophy majors and six Spanish majors took the Graduate Record Exams provided by the ETS.

The three-hour exams, which were administered by the Ohio Wesleyan Evaluation Service, make up the written portion of the students' comprehensives. Oral tests will be given at a later time set up by each department.

Five elementary education majors graduating in February also took the Teacher Education Exams provided by the E.T.S.

In other departments, exams are being made up by members of the University staff. Three journalism majors graduating in February took their exams yesterday,

articles.headline: Social Fee Tax Added
articles.body:
A three cent admissions tax is being charged on OWU's newly initiated Social Fee by the city of Delaware, according to Student Body Treasurer Dick Smith. The tax will take $180 from the Student Government budget, but will not draw from the special fund.

OWU students have been paying a city admissions tax on activities ever since Delaware took over the tax in 1947, when it was dropped by the state, Kenneth Bachtel, Delaware finance director, said. "In the past, tax was included in the admission," he explained, "and since the activities fee is an admission charge, it is equally taxable by Delaware city law."

Since the student body voted to spend the $3 per person charge on activities, with no provision for a tax deduction, the tax will be paid with a portion of the money that has in the past been allotted to the Social Committee, he said.

articles.headline: Ohio Will Play Key Role In '60 Presidential Race
articles.body:
The state of Ohio will continue to be in the political headlines from now until the presidential elections next fall. Ohio is traditionally one of the four key states in the nation, the others being New York, California and Illinois.

OHIO IS ONE of 16 states which use the presidential primary, and in addition uses the presidential preference vote and direct election of delegates to the national convention.

This election will see Ohio's delegates pledged as a bloc for John Kennedy of Massachusetts, according to Governor DiSalle.

The Republican position in Ohio appears to be firmly established, with Vice-President Nixon's name to definitely appear on the primary ballot May 3. State Auditor James A. Rhodes, the only Republican in Ohio state office seeking re-election in 1960, has agreed to the use of his name as second choice on the slate.

The GOP scene in Ohio, as elsewhere, is relatively easy to understand, now that Nelson Rockefeller has declined to campaign for the nomination. In direct contrast, at least nationally, is the Democratic situation, with its multitude of candidates and potential candidates.

GOVERNOR MICHAEL DISALLE has endorsed Senator Kennedy for the Democratic presidential nomination. DiSalle will campaign as a favorite son, pledged to Kennedy's candidacy, thereby securing Ohio's bloc of delegates for the Massachusetts senator.

DiSalle's early declaration of intention may have been rather hasty, however, since complete support of the Ohio delegation is not yet assured. Senator Frank Lausche, with his contingent of Cleveland delegates, does not appear to be solidly seated on the DiSalle (i.e. Kennedy) bandwagon.

DiSalle has declared that "Kennedy is the popular choice of the Democratic voters of Ohio," but the Massachusetts senator's backing within the party is perhaps not as solid as DiSalle would like to think.

MISSOURI'S SENATOR STUART Symington appears to be the number one man in the eyes of Carmine De Sapio, New York's national committeeman and state Democratic boss, and Michael Prendergast, Missouri's Democratic state chairman.

Symington has few enemies and has offended no bloc of voters; he has successfully straddled the political fence and is well-liked by labor.

Also definitely a threat to Kennedy's aspirations is the figure of Adlai Stevenson, who is apparently backed by the Reform Democrats in general and by Eleanor Roosevelt in particular. Stevenson's national popularity is not as week as his "0-for-two" presidential won-lost record might indicate.

IN THE EYES OF MANY Americans, Stevenson's intellectualism is still an outstanding trait, while his foreign travels have added to his prominance both here and abroad. In general, Stevenson — although twice defeated — is an image of strength to many Democrats, and may even be said to be the titular head of his party.

It is obvious, therefore, that Ohio's role in the national political picture is not wholly resolved. And finally, as election time draws nearer, we again emphasize that college students have a responsibility as citizens, whether they are of voting age or not, to fully acquaint themsleves with the candidates and issues at stake.

articles.headline: Telephone Call 'Pranks' Involve Criminal Act
articles.body:
In the past two years the practice of charging long-distance telephone calls to phone numbers other than their own has arisen among a number of students. The numbers given are usually those of another fraternity. Some fraternities have been forced to pay several hundred dollars per year for these calls of "unknown origin."

PERHAPS THE INDIVIDUALS involved are not aware that this practice is a violation of both state and federal laws. Recently the Northern Ohio Telephone Co. has begun tracing all calls of this nature to discover the individuals responsible.

The company's findings are being reported to the University, and charges are being pressed in Men's Court by the Administration. Recent cases have resulted in heavy fines being levied against the guilty parties.

The reason for such acts is undoubtedly a combination of factors. First, most fraternity houses, to protect themselves, do not permit their members to make long-distance calls charged to the house. Second, such acts are often rationalized as "pranks" upon a rival Greek group, and probably sometimes are spontaneous acts of this nature.

articles.headline: Prejudice
articles.author: Holly Sprague
articles.body:
Editor, the Transcript:

At Athens, Ohio, an international, interracial interdenominational group learned recently how peoples and persons have dreams of life and of freedom. We learned further how other nations and persons, including Russia, Great Britain the United States, and to our discomfort each one of us, can frustrate these dreams and ruin people's lives.

The group became aware that "democratic" Western nations have taught democracy to "backward" countries of Asia and Africa, and then have taken away their freedom.

Many international students at the Conference testified to their desire for the independence of their own people and their zeal to prove by gaining freedom that they are people who are not inferior to the "Christian West."

What Is Outcome?

"What happens to a dream deferred? . Does it EXPLODE? . Does it make no difference to us that they are giving their lives in a desperate struggle while we in our American complacency are not even interested?"

The forces of racial prejudice are everywhere present. While we are apathetic in our OWU ivory tower, these forces seek Americans are inferior, not truly people.

Sometimes their logic goes something like this:
(1) All men are created in the image of God. (2) God is not a Negro. (3) Therefore, the Negro is not a man.

Statement Made

Honest statements were made - by a student from Nigeria who was told when seeking quarters in the United States that he must understand that here in America Negroes are not to associate with whites; by a white student from the South who admitted her prejudice and told of her struggle against it; by Southern Negroes and Northern Negroes; by sociologists; by Dr. Martin Luther King.

While prejudice is allowed to ruin the lives of people, in Delaware as well as in Little Rock, whose frustration has no escape and no hope, we often do not even notice.

As a group we grappled with the problem of other religions, asking whether Christianity is unique. Soon we discovered that these religions exist not only in Asia and Africa, but also in each of us: Our desire for a neat philosophical system makes us Hindu; our seeking for an ethical code to tell us how to live is Buddhist, not Christian.

Not a Religion

It was suggested that the uniqueness of Christianity is that Christianity is not a religion; man's religion is his attempt to justify himself in relation to others and to God, while Christianity proclaims that God accepts man as he is.

We did not come to any final conclusions at the Conference, and we left somewhat bewildered - where in the world is God today? All of us experienced, however, a sense of his presence, that somehow God is working.

We left having discovered that there are other people in the world besides us, that they have concern for anyone but ourselves we can help - by interest and by courage to stand for truth in all areas of human struggle.

articles.headline: Right To Strike Must Be Preserved
articles.author: Jerry Sell
articles.body:
Richard Nixon's recent action in solving the steel strike has taken the administration off a very dangerous hook.

If the strike had resumed, increasing pressure on the government would almost certainly have forced Eisenhower to take some drastic step to send the men permanently back to the mills.

The methods suggested have ranged from compulsory arbitration to cries for legislation forbidding strikes in the steel industry.

Outcome Fortunate
It is fortunate that in this situation the government didn't have to take such action. However, it seems likely that some day the same situation may come up again.

If the government does take any such steps restricting the right to strike, it will be one of the most unfortunate things a United States government has ever done.

Labor has come in this country from a state of near-peonage to a position of respect and power and equity before management only because of its ability to hurt industry with crippling strikes.

Force Was Necessary
The only reason companies have generally yielded equitable treatment to workers has been because they have been forced to.

What the recent complaints over the steel strike really say is: It should be illegal to stage an effective strike; that is, one that really seriously hurts the national economy.

True the argument that the national defense was threatened small portion of steel production goes into defense work.

Anything Hurts
In fact, the crippling of almost any major industry can be said to hurt national defense.

No, the freedom to strike, above all the freedom to achieve a successful strike, one that hurts, must be protected by all means!

If that right is taken away, the American worker will have lost the only major weapon which has enabled him to attain his rightful place in American society.

articles.headline: Greek Troubles
articles.body:
Editor, the Transcript:
Are Wesleyan's Greek-letter organizations really fulfilling a worthwhile purpose? Is the "club" merely a place to hang one's hat, have parties, and waste time playing bridge or does it have some significant function in enriching the student's life?

These questions are a few of many concerning this topic under debate by faculty and students alike.

There appear to be three major complaints against the fraternity system. First, they are divisive. Students are apt to feel more loyalty to their fraternities or sororities than to their university.

Grouping Is Natural
Is this actually furthered by the organizations in question, or is this grouping together an inescapable quality of human nature? It is my belief that the latter is true.

Secondly, it is felt that those involuntarily excluded from the organization of their choice will be seriously harmed both socially and emotionally.

This is a good point, yet is it not true that most people find their special group of friends? Isn't it true also that the student accepted in a fraternity because of alumni pressure will be harmed even more when he is socially unacceptable to his own group? I feel that it is.

Un-Americanism? The third factor is the charge of being un-American in policies of racial and religious discrimination. This, I feel, is the greatest cause of dissention.

Trueblood says in his book The Idea of a College that merely because this discrimination is found outside the college campus, it shouldn't be condoned, because, "the college exists not to reflect but to challenge the world."

Discrimination is incompatible with the principles of a Christian college. This is a major point in the attitude of Wesleyan's students.

Student Lack
It seems that many of these students are incapable of thinking for themselves and if they manage to reach this point they can't stand up for the things they believe in.

Conformity is the rule: conform or be ostracized. Fraternal organizations originally purported brotherhood; now they enforce a social stigma upon certain individuals.

These three are probably the most important causes of dissention, but there are many ways in which Greek organizations do make contributions to the lives of the students.

Lends Confidence
To the entering freshman, the social acceptance he finds in a fraternity gives him confidence. Although this may be a disputed attribute, the Greek organization tries to provide the academic motivation the student may lack until he finds himself and his real goals.

There is no reason why Wesleyan students are incapable of fighting these basic complaints. Granted, it may be impossible to create the ideal fraternity situation, but great strides can be made if a few more students would give a little time and thought to the improvement of their individual group.

If our Greek organizations are to continue in their existence, it is time for us to prove that there is meaning behind them. Marilyn Redman

articles.headline: LITTLE STORIES WITH BIG MORALS
articles.author: with Max Shulman
articles.body:
(Author of "I Was a Teen-age Dwarf" "The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis", etc.)

First Little Story
Once upon a time a German exchange student from old Heidelberg came to an American university. He lived in the men's dormitory of the great American university. He was a fine, decent young man and all the other young men in the dormitory of the great American university tried very hard to make friends with him, but, unfortunately, he was so shy that he refused all their invitations to join their bull sessions. After a while his dormitory mates got tired of asking him and so the poor German exchange student, alas, spent every evening alone in his room.

One night while sitting all alone in his room, he smelled the most delicious aroma coming from the room next door. Conquering his shyness, he walked to the room next door and there he saw a bunch of his dormitory mates sitting around and discussing literature, art, culture, and like that. They were all smoking Marlboro cigarettes, which accounts for the delicious aroma smelled by the German exchange student.

Timidly, he entered the room. "Excuse me," he said, "but what is that marvelous smell I smell?"

"It's our good Marlboro cigarettes," cried the men, who were named Fun-loving Ned, Happy Harry, Jolly Jim, and Tol'able David.

So the German exchange student took a Marlboro and enjoyed those better makin's, that finer filter, that smooth, hearty flavor, and soon he was comfortable and easy and lost his shyness.

From that night forward, whenever he smelled the good smell of Marlboro cigarettes, he always went next door and joined the bull session.

MORAL: WHERE THERE'S SMOKE, THERE'S MEYER

Second Little Story
Once upon a time there was an Indian brave named Walter T. Muskrat who had a squaw named Margaret Giggling Water. Margaret was sort of a mess but she sure could make beaded moccasins. Every day she whipped up a brand-new pair of beaded moccasins for Walter, which were so gorgeous that all the Indian maids on the reservation grew giddy with admiration.

Well, sir, Margaret got pretty tense about all the girls making eyes at Walter and one night they had a terrible quarrel. Walter flew into a rage and slapped her on the wrist, whereupon she started crying like all get-out and went home to her mother and never came back.

"Good riddance!" said Walter, but alas, he soon found out how wrong he was, for the Indian maids were not really interested in him, only in his moccasins, and when he stopped showing up with a new pair every day they quickly gave him the yo-heave-ho. Today he is a broken man, sitting all alone in his tepee and muttering ancient Ute curses.

MORAL: DON'T FIGHT THE HAND THAT BEADS YOU

Third Little Story
Once there was a lion which was a very quiet lion. In fact, the only time it ever made a sound was when it had a toothache.

articles.headline: Council Gets Phone Plan
articles.body:
A report writing student's plan to improve the University phone system has been submitted to Student Council, Council President Bryce Collier said last week.

Leedom Kettell, a student in Assistant Professor of English Libuse Reed's English 203 (Report Writing) class, made the report as a class assignment, and also submitted it to Student Council.

Collier has asked Kettell to do further research on the situation as a special Council project and to report his findings to the group.

Kettell's report stressed the need for 10-20 new phones in the three women's dorms, the use of pay phones for long distance calls, and the exercising of courtesy in using the phones.

"The biggest problem in this situation is definitely the cost," Kettell admitted. There is room for 39 more extensions on the University switchboard, but the smaller switchboards in the dorms would need to be supplemented if any additional phones are to be installed, he reported.

Kettell is planning to find the exact cost of the equipment and maintenance before he submits a further report to Council. He said that the telephone operators in the dorms were in favor of the extra phones, and that they did not think it would make their jobs any harder.

"If nothing else," he concluded, "I hope the Student Council can push this idea of courteousness in phoning. This won't cost the school anything, and it could ease the situation quite a lot."

articles.headline: 'Orchard' Blossoms For Canadian Actors
articles.author: Jo Ann Kiser
articles.body:
"The Cherry Orchard" was in full bloom last Wednesday when the Canadian Players made an even more impressive showing in their return with Chekhov than in their successful presentation of "The Devil's Disciple" last year.

The play is symbolic of the end of the anachronistic gentry and the emergence of the middle class in Russia. The widow, Mme. Ranevskaya, and her brother Gaev are representative of the effete Russian gentry. Jacquelin Barnett played the slightly overwritten part of the widow to perfection, portraying the charm and foolishly inadequate generosity intended by Chekhov.

Her brother, Claude Bede, is similar, with Bede proclaiming the irrationally optimistic speeches of the bewildered gentleman who fights reality. The emergence of the middle class is symbolized by Lopahin, characterized by Max Helpmann, as the son of a serf, ever surprised and uncertain of his new-found power as a rich merchant.

The peasant role is made richer by the side plot of Lopahin's mutual love with the widow's adopted daughter Varya. Nun-like Varya (Tudi Wiggins) is the most wistful character in the play, so obvious in her attraction for Lopahin, yet turning her back when he enters the room.

The other romantic plot involves the student, Trofimov (John Gardiner), who portrays the third important group of Chekhov's Russia, the young, self-supposed intellectuals of the time who see and welcome the coming change and yet are inevitably bound somewhat to the old way of life.

His love affair with the widow's daughter (delicately played by Bena Shuter) and their willingness to "live the new life" provides the only happy ending in the play.

The binding thread in the play is the whacky governess Charlotta Ivanova (Barbara Hamilton), who is the spectator looking on uninvolved, perhaps Chekhov's mouthpiece in the play.

Miss Hamilton did extremely well in the part. Had anyone's attention been distracted for some reason from the main spectators in the leaving scene, she would have thrown them into nervous hysterics, standing there with the ridiculous hat pulled over one eye and the mock tragedy of her position, her high firm nose "ever higher and higher into the air."

A character part was played by Charles Palmer as Firs, the old valet still bound to his masters, considering the great day of misfortune as the day when the serfs were freed. His dying at the end symbolizes the definite end of an era and just as he dies, the cutting down of the first cherry tree is heard in the orchard.

Part of the theatrical atmosphere was provided by the players' custom of changing scenery openly between acts and their ingenious transformations in so doing, such as changing a table into a well.

It wouldn't be a bad idea for the Lecture-Movie Series to continue the habit of making the Canadian Players a yearly attraction.

articles.headline: OWU Hosts Debate Trial
articles.body:
The annual Ohio Wesleyan invitational debate tournament was held here last Saturday, sponsored by the OWU chapter of Delta Sigma Rho, national speech honor society.

Sixteen colleges and universities from Ohio and nearby states took part in the competition, reported Edward R. Robinson, associate professor of speech and director of forensics at OWU. Ohio University won the tournament, winning six and losing none in the three rounds of debates.

Ohio Wesleyan "used beginning debaters," said Prof. Robinson, so that they might gain experience in actual competitive debate situations. OWU won only two of six debates, Prof. Robinson added.

Charlie Mills and Gus Hemmett, debating against the University of Cincinnati, and Fred Manske and Bob Carlson, debating against Capital, scored the only two victories for Ohio Wesleyan.

Schools participating in the tournament, according to Prof. Robinson, were Bluffton, Bowling Green, Capital, Cincinnati, Dayton, Findlay, Heidelberg, Marietta, Marshall, Muskingum, Ohio State, Ohio University, Ohio Wesleyan, Otterbein, Pittsburgh and Wittenberg.

articles.headline: Perkins Scope Slated For Arizona Relocation
articles.body:
The 69-inch reflecting telescope at Perkins Observatory will be moved late this year to a site near Flagstaff, Ariz., where weather conditions will permit greater use of the instrument, the fifth largest reflector in the United States.

The move has been under consideration for more than two years, and the agreement was concluded between Ohio Wesleyan (owners of the telescope), Ohio State University (co-users) and the Lowell Observatory (soon to be the site of the instrument).

The move, financially underwritten by the National Science Foundation to the tune of $273,000, is being made to make more efficient research use of the instrument. Visibility, due to atmospheric distortion and nearby lights, is poor in the Columbus-Delaware area, limiting use of the telescope to relatively few nights per year. The Arizona site will improve these conditions by about four times.

Members of the astronomy departments of Ohio Wesleyan and Ohio State will continue to be able to use the instrument for their research observations, and a 32-inch scope, donated to OWU by Michael R. Schottland of Martinsville, Va., will be placed in Perkins Observatory. In addition a 16-inch photographic scope will also be installed here. Ohio Wesleyan will retain ownership of the large telescope after the move to Arizona, with the Lowell staff charged with maintenance.

The 69-inch instrument was presented to Ohio Wesleyan in 1931 by Prof. Hiram Perkins, who taught astronomy here. Its reflecting mirror, produced at the Bureau of Standards, was the first large mirror cast in this country. The telescope itself was built and installed by the Warner and Swasey Co. of Cleveland, O.

articles.headline: Springfield City Post To Stilwell
articles.body:
Roger Stilwell, who has served as Delaware city manager for the past three and a half years, recently resigned his post to become city manager in Springfield, O.

Stilwell, who presented his formal resignation to City Council on Dec. 14, explained that the only reason he is leaving Delaware is to fill the vacant position in Springfield. He will assume his new post Jan. 18.

Stilwell also remarked that City Council is presently accepting applications for the vacated position which he has occupied since July, 1956.

During an interview with the Transcript, Stilwell commented, "I have spent three and a half valuable and enjoyable years of service in Delaware. I particularly regret leaving the community because I feel Delaware is on the verge of a great economic advancement.

Of course, Ohio Wesleyan has always been a stabilizing influence upon the economy of the community. Also because several new industries are moving to Delaware, I feel there will be a marked increase in the prosperity of the city."

articles.headline: 'Messiah' Available
articles.body:
Orders are being taken for recordings of Handel's "Messiah," preformed in December by the A Cappella Choir, Men's and Women's Glee Clubs and the OWU Symphony Orchestra.

The recordings were made with the cooperation of the Music Department.

The records, which are 33 1/3 LP recordings, can be ordered in all of the women's dormitories, men's residence halls, the MUB and Gray Chapel. According to John Race, approximately 130 orders have been sold already out of the 500 expected.

A few extra copies will be on sale after the present order arrives near the end of January, he said.

articles.headline: Sorority To Build
articles.body:
After five years of planning, Kappa Alpha Theta sorority will get a new home. President Sue Shidaker said Sunday that construction of the building will begin Mar. 1 on the same site as their present lodge at 179 West Winter St.

The old house will be vacated Jan. 25, although its actual fate is as yet undecided, she declared. It will either be bought and moved from the Winter Street location or razed by Feb. 15. "Two or three buyers" are negotiating for the structure, Miss Shidaker said.

The sorority has occupied the house since 1946, but the need for more space, functional rooms and sturdier foundations led to the move. "It is a very old house," she commented.

A Columbus firm has the contract for the $55,000 structure, Miss Shidaker said.

The sorority will be temporarily housed in the Old Nurses Home behind Austin Hall, according to arrangements made by University Treasurer D. J. Hornberger, she remarked.

articles.headline: Press Box
articles.author: Rog Lockwood
articles.body:
The recent explosions concerning quiz show frauds and disk jockey "payola" have awakened America to a new kind of approach to life. Instead of continuing in the time-worn tradition of shading the truth, public figures seem now to be going out of their way to be brutally honest.

The case in point is a statement made a short time ago by Duffy Daugherty, Michigan State football coach. Said he:

"Our grants-in-aid are awarded for academic achievement and need-By academic achievement - if he can read and write. By need - well, we don't take a boy unless we need him."

Thus, the Michigan State coach may have started a trend which would be very interesting to see develop at Ohio Wesleyan.

Imagine, if you will, the Bishop coaching staff following Daugherty's lead. The result might be something like this:

Track Coach: "Don't call me Gee. The name is Geesman. Mr. Geesman, to you!"

And . .

Humanities Prof: "Final exams are necessary and valuable. By necessary - so you will cram. By valuable - so I'll have an excuse for flunking you."

Chapel Committeeman: "Chapel programs are designed to fulfill your spiritual and educational needs. By spiritual — sleep is a blessing. By educational — where else is more studying, knitting and letter-writing done?"

College President: "I am confident that our building program will provide us with the best facilities anywhere. By building program - a new hiding place for Lee. By anywhere - anywhere in Delaware, Ohio."

But, getting back to Daugherty, it would be interesting to have some of the other member schools in the Ohio Conference shed the light of truth on their athlete admissions and subsidation policies.

"Some schools in the OC spend a lot of time getting good athletes. By time - money."

articles.headline: Tom Eibel Athlete of the Week
articles.body:
Tom Eibel has been named Athlete of the Week for the second time in his sports career here at Ohio Wesleyan. He was chosen by the coaching staff and sports publicist for his outstanding performance in the Denison game Saturday night.

Against the Big Red, Eibel bucketed 10 points and led the Bishops with his agressive defensive play and pinpointing passes which set up numerous Bishop baskets.

While Eibel is only 5 ft. 9 in. tall he led the Bishops with 11 rebounds. That total has been surpassed only four times this season by his taller teammates. Eibel's clutch play was also a key part of the cagers fourth victory. In the last two minutes of play he dribbled the ball for 40 sec. and drew two fouls, He cashed in on the charity shots insuring the Bishops of their slim five point margin.

articles.headline: Grapplers Win Opener
articles.author: Bill Bishop
articles.body:
With George Menges posting his 15th straight victory as an OWU wrestler, the Bishop grapplers downed Marshall College by a 16-14 score in a meet held there Dec. 18.

With the score tied 11-11, Menges, captain of the squad, defeated his 177 lb. opponent by pinning him in the second period of their match. The pin, worth five points, gave OWU a 16-11 lead which, despite a gain of three points by Marshall when heavyweight Ed Metz was decisioned, was enough for the victory.

Also pinning his man was 157 lb. John Tilton. Tilton, a returning letterman, shouldered his adversary in the second period.

Other winners for the Bishops were 137 lb. Bert Laub and 167 lb. Dave Williams. Laub, who won 8-0, wrestled a near-perfect match while Williams, a freshman, dominated the mat while gaining a 12-3 decision.

The grapplers' lack of experience in the lower weight classes was apparent as 123 lb. Lewis Jones and 130 lb. Clint Strong lost decisions and 147 lb. Dick Williamson was pinned.

This Thursday at 4 p.m. Kenyon will visit Edwards Gym for a meet, and Denison will be here at 1:30 p. m. Saturday. Both matches should be close and the wrestling team deserves good student support.

articles.headline: OWU Swimmers Rip Past Muskingum; Brown, Dickey Set School Records
articles.author: Bob Moyers
articles.body:
After easily downing Muskingum, 70-24, last Saturday, Ohio Wesleyan's swimming team heads after bigger game against Wittenberg's Tigers today at Springfield O., and the Bearcats of Cincinnati O., here Friday at 4 p. m.

Coached by Dave Maurer, Wittenberg finished third in this year's Ohio Conference Relays, only 15 points behind OWU.

Coach Dick Gordin stated that the Tigers are strong in the distances and they have a fine backstroker in Faggly, the conference champ. Gordin also commented about freshman divers Dave Cunningham and George Collins, who finished second in the relays.

"It will be a good test for us," remarked Gordin, "and it should be a pretty good meet."

Face Cincy Friday
On Friday, the Bishop tankers will host Cincinnati, the Missouri Valley Conference champions. The non-conference meet will be the final action for Gordin's splashers until after finals.

Last Saturday's decisive victory over Muskingum produced two new OWU records. Jim Brown, OWU recordholder in the 200-yard butterfly, clipped 2 seconds off his own record with a time of 2:30.2.

The other record occured when Jerry Dickey lowered his own OWU mark in the 200-yard breaststroke with a time of 2:42 for the event.

The OWU swimmers took 10 firsts in the 11-event program to easily dominate the meet. The only Muskie victory came in the diving where Ruba took first place.

Ken Potter, Muskingum's coach, attributed the fine balance of the OWU team as the reason for the defeat. He also stated that Ohio Wesleyan should have a fine chance to take the conference crown this year.

articles.headline: Shannon To Head Group
articles.body:
Ohio Wesleyan's basketball coach, Frank Shannon, has been elected chairman of the newly formed Ohio Conference Basketball Association. Wooster's Jim Ewers was elected vice-chairman.

The association was formed in an effort to achieve more complete uniformity within the league and promote basketball on a conference level.

All coaches in the OC will participate in the association, which will serve in an advisory capacity to the league basketball committee and the athletic directors.

Among specific problems being considered by the coaches are officiating, scheduling, and details of the OC and NCAA tournaments.

The OC tourney will be held for the first time this year, with all 14 colleges participating in an elimination series of games.

The league has been divided into a North and South section, with the seven southern teams, including OWU, competing at Capital and seven northern teams at Akron, Feb. 26 and 27.

Two teams will emerge from each section for the finals to be held at Akron March 4-5. After this season the tourney winner will represent the Ohio Conference at the NCAA college division championships.

articles.headline: Cagers Trounce Otterbein, Denison; Meet Lawrence Tech Here Tonight
articles.author: Tom Grissom
articles.body:
After knocking off Otterbein, 93-67, and nudging Denison, 79-74, the Bishop cagers face two non-conference opponents in games this week.

The Bishops will meet Lawrence Tech from Detroit on the Edwards Gym hardwood at 8 p.m. tonight. The invading Blue Devils are a young squad with only one senior listed on the roster and three frosh on the varsity. OWU expects them to be an aggressive, fast-breaking unit with plenty of scoring punch.

Team leader and high scorer is Clayton Pethers, a 6 ft. 5 in. sophomore, who has been hitting at a 22 point clip per game. Against Otterbein this season he tallied 46 points. His coach, George Verdonckt, calls him "a great ballplayer and dangerous from anywhere on the floor."

Last year Lawrence posted a 13-14 slate. Tonight's meeting between these two teams in their first encounter and is rated a toss-up.

Meet Morris Harvey Saturday

Saturday the Golden Eagles from Morris Harvey provide the opposition for the Bishop netmen. The contest is scheduled for 8 p.m. at Edwards Gym.

The West Virginians boast of a 7-4 won and lost record so far this year and hope to equal last year's slate of 15-6. The Eagles have five men who averaged in double figures last year returning to the present squad. Don Stover is top scorer of the team, with a 17.4 average to his credit. He is closely followed by teammate Denny Skiles, who maintains a 16-point scoring rate.

Whip Denison, 79-74

Cheered on by a large group of "spiritous" followers, the Red and Black cagers repulsed a late rally to defeat Denison, 79-74, last Saturday night.

The Bishops piled up a 13-point margin mid-way through the first half but it dwindled to three points, 41-38, at intermission. In the second half the referee's whistle almost decided the game for the two teams. Both squads lost their top scorers because of excess fouls and OWU's accuracy at the foul line provided the final advantage. Each team made 28 field goals but OWU outscored the Big Red 23-18 at the foul line.

The Bishops had five men in double figures, with Tom Nims high scorer with 26. Ray Slabaugh and Jerry Vaughn each got 14. Bill Miller tallied 12 points and Tom Eibel notched 10.

Weddell High Scorer For Big Red

High scorer for Denison was Jerry Weddell with 19. Teammate Tom Edwards followed with 17.

Coach Shannon was highly impressed with the team's showing and credited them and aggressiveness!" He added with "a great deal of desire his pleasure at the attendance of OWU students at the game. Said Shannon, "both the team and I want to express our thanks to the students who followed and supported us so well at Denison."

Roll Over Otterbein

The Bishops avenged an early season loss by walloping the visiting Cardinals from Otterbein, 93-67, last Thursday night.

Starting slowly, the cagers led at halftime, 39-35. In the second half the Bishops began to click. Within a few minutes they raced to a 66-51 score and were never in trouble the rest of the night. Ray Spears was high scorer for the Otters with 18 points.

This headline accompanies the main sports coverage detailed in the primary article regarding the basketball team's recent victories.

articles.body:

Prof. Alter will be vice-president of the department, which has about 600 members, for one year. It is one of seven departments in the O.E.A.

articles.headline: USAF Dubs Berman Captain
articles.body:
Leonard J. Berman, assistant professor of air science, was promoted to captain in the United States Air Force, Jan. 1.

Prof. Berman came to Ohio Wesleyan in July, 1957, from France, where he had been stationed since 1954.

A 1952 graduate of Ohio University, Prof. Berman obtained his M.S. degree from New York University. He was commissioned in 1953 and went on active duty in 1954, at which time he attended Personnel Officers' School.
